source: Tao et al. (2024) Cultural bias and cultural alignment of LLMs, PNAS Nexus
finding: Five GPT models answered ten World Values Survey items. All sat near English-speaking and Protestant European countries, far from African-Islamic ones.
numbers: 107 countries/territories, 10 prompt variants per item. GPT-4o closest to New Zealand d=0.98, Iceland d=0.97, Australia d=0.86; farthest Jordan d=4.10, Libya d=4.00, Ghana d=3.95.
limits: Only ten survey items; survey values, not reasoning processes. WVS/EVS data are themselves self-report.
agent_relevance: A default model is one cultural sample. Evidence it gives about what people think must be weighted as WEIRD-leaning.

source: Tao et al. (2024) Cultural bias and cultural alignment of LLMs, PNAS Nexus
finding: Cultural prompting ('You are an average human born in [country]') cut distance to the target country for newer models.
numbers: Mean distance: GPT-4o 2.42 to 1.57; GPT-4-turbo 2.71 to 1.77; GPT-4 2.69 to 1.65 (Wilcoxon P<0.001). Improved for 71-81% of countries for GPT-4/4-turbo/4o. Less effective for GPT-3/3.5.
limits: Still 19-29% of countries not improved; survey items only; persona may encode stereotype.
agent_relevance: A one-line persona is a cheap, measurable scaffold. It shifts stated values, not proven reasoning.

source: Tao et al. (2024) Cultural bias and cultural alignment of LLMs, PNAS Nexus
finding: Value position moved across model versions without a trend: GPT-3.5-turbo and 4o more secular, 4-turbo more traditional, GPT-3 and GPT-4 near global average.
numbers: Kruskal-Wallis across models P=0.036 on bias distribution (barely significant).
limits: Authors only speculate that RLHF and rule-based rewards explain the shifts; training data undisclosed.
agent_relevance: Cultural lean is not stable across versions; any claim about a model's culture needs re-testing per version.

source: Cao et al. (2023) Assessing cross-cultural alignment between ChatGPT and human societies
finding: ChatGPT matched American survey answers best; other cultures aligned better only when asked in the local language, and unreliably.
numbers: Hofstede-style survey, 5 cultures (US, CN, DE, JP, ES), 3 prompts. Spearman prompt 1: US 0.70 (p=0.12), CN -0.77 (p=0.07), DE -0.66 (p=0.16). Prompts 1&2 combined for ES 0.93 (p=0.01).
limits: Only 5 cultures, so most correlations are not significant. Early ChatGPT (2023).
agent_relevance: Small-n culture comparisons are fragile. Treat sign flips between prompts as noise, not culture.

source: Cao et al. (2023) Assessing cross-cultural alignment between ChatGPT and human societies
finding: Injecting correct cultural knowledge in a multi-turn exchange shifted answers; irrelevant text did not; false 'knowledge' was accepted.
numbers: Table 6 response scores: original 1.5, correct description 2.5, non-relevant 3.5, incorrect description 1.0. Same item moved from 'utmost important' (English prompt) to 'moderate' (Japanese prompt).
limits: Scores on the paper's own scale; one case study.
agent_relevance: Models believe injected context, even wrong context. A scaffold that adds cultural context needs a check on that context.

source: Durmus et al. (2023) Towards measuring the representation of subjective global opinions in language models
finding: GlobalOpinionQA (Pew and World Values Survey questions): default answers resembled USA, Canada, Australia, some European and South American respondents.
numbers: Three conditions: default, cross-national prompting, linguistic prompting.
limits: One Constitutional-AI model only; opinion distributions, not cognition.
agent_relevance: Default answers are not a neutral human average.

source: Durmus et al. (2023) Towards measuring the representation of subjective global opinions in language models
finding: Telling the model to answer as a country's people moved answers toward that country but produced stereotypes; asking in Russian, Chinese or Turkish did not move answers toward those speakers.
numbers: Example: asked in Russian the model stayed closer to US/Canada/Europe than Russia. Model did the translating.
limits: LLM translation may lose nuance; authors admit this.
agent_relevance: Prompt language is a weak lever; explicit persona is stronger but stereotype-prone. Do not claim a model thinks in a language.

source: Naous et al. (2024) Having beer after prayer? Measuring cultural bias in LLMs (CAMeL)
finding: 16 models, even Arabic-only models, prefer Western entities in Arabic prompts (names, food, drinks). Multilingual models show more Western bias than monolingual ones.
numbers: CAMeL: 628 prompts, 20,368 entities, 8 types. Cultural Bias Score 40-65% for all LMs (lower = less Western preference).
limits: Entity-level bias, not reasoning style; Wikipedia-derived entity lists.
agent_relevance: Prompt language does not remove source culture. Arabic text is itself Western-heavy.

source: Naous et al. (2024) Having beer after prayer? Measuring cultural bias in LLMs (CAMeL)
finding: Prepending Arab-context demonstrations lowered Western bias for most models; a special culture token barely helped.
numbers: Qualitative in text: demonstrations reduced CBS for most LMs; culture token little effect. Exact drop not recorded.
limits: Exact reduction not extracted.
agent_relevance: In-context examples beat labels. Use worked local examples, not flags.

source: Masoud et al. (2024) Cultural alignment in LLMs: Hofstede's dimensions
finding: Llama 2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 tested on Hofstede dimensions for US, China and Arab countries. All struggle; GPT-4 adapts best for China, worst for US and Arab; fine-tuning Llama 2 in a language changes cultural answers.
numbers: Three models x three regions x several prompt styles.
limits: Hofstede is a contested country-level scheme.
agent_relevance: Hofstede-based scores are the weak standard of this literature. Weigh them lightly.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Not all countries celebrate Thanksgiving: cultural dominance in LLMs
finding: Asked in non-English languages, GPT models give English-culture answers; GPT-4 most affected, text-davinci-003 least.
numbers: Benchmark across 11 languages, concrete (holidays, songs) and abstract (values) objects. ERNIE in-culture score on concrete Chinese items 7.6 vs GPT-4 1.8.
limits: Fix is partial.
agent_relevance: Stronger models can be more culturally dominated. Capability is not neutrality.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Not all countries celebrate Thanksgiving: cultural dominance in LLMs
finding: Two cheap fixes helped: pretrain on more local data, or add 'In the culture of [lang], ...' or 'consider the culture associated with the query language'.
numbers: Two prompts P1, P2 tested; per-language gains in paper tables, not extracted.
limits: Exact gains not extracted.
agent_relevance: A one-sentence cultural cue is a cost-free scaffold.

source: Rao et al. (2025) NormAd: cultural adaptability of LLMs
finding: Models judge social acceptability worse for Global South cultures than English-speaking ones, and worse when only abstract values are given.
numbers: 2.6k stories, 75 countries. With explicit rule-of-thumb: best models <82% vs humans >95%. With value or country only: models <60%, humans >90%.
limits: Etiquette norms only; story format.
agent_relevance: Humans reason from context to norms easily; models need the rule written out. Provide the rule.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) WorldValuesBench
finding: Predicting WVS answers from demographics is hard. Share of questions within Wasserstein distance 0.2 of the human distribution is low for small models.
numbers: 94,728 participants, 20 million+ examples. Alpaca-7B 11.1%, Vicuna-7B 25.0%, Mixtral-8x7B 72.2%, GPT-3.5 Turbo 75.0%.
limits: Demographic-conditioned rating task, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Useful for judging whether a persona claim is trustworthy.

source: Jin et al. (2025) Language model alignment in multilingual trolley problems (MultiTP)
finding: 19 LLMs on Moral Machine style dilemmas in 107 languages: alignment with human judgments varies widely by language; models miss variation, e.g. always prefer humans over animals.
numbers: 460 English vignettes x 107 languages; 6 moral dimensions; Moral Machine has 40 million+ judgments from 200+ countries.
limits: Google Translate used; not human-checked in every language.
agent_relevance: Same dilemma, different language, different answer: no cross-language invariance, which a universal reasoner would show.

source: Kharchenko et al. (2025) How well do LLMs represent values across cultures?
finding: With personas of 36 countries/languages, models separate cultural values in classification but do not hold them consistently when giving advice.
numbers: Hofstede dimensions as basis; a correlation of -0.527 reported for low-resource languages vs 0.314 for another group (context in paper tables).
limits: Persona prompts; advice judged by classifier.
agent_relevance: Knowing a value is not acting on it. Check outputs, do not trust a stated persona.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: On NLI, syllogisms and Wason selection, models and humans both do better when content fits belief and worse when it conflicts with logic. This fits the claim of a shared, content-bound reasoning style.
numbers: Three tasks, humans vs several LMs; effect shown as accuracy gap between content-supports and content-conflicts.
limits: Western online participants; no cross-cultural human sample.
agent_relevance: Content effects look near-universal in humans and appear in LLMs, so a scaffold should test logic on abstract versions of a problem.

source: Atari, Xue, Park, Blasi, Henrich (2023) Which humans?
finding: GPT answers on psychological measures sit in the WEIRD corner. Fit falls fast with distance from WEIRD populations.
numbers: r = -.70 between performance and distance from WEIRD populations (abstract only).
limits: Only the abstract and search commentary seen; triad task details not verified.
agent_relevance: Core evidence that LLM = Westerner is a sampling issue. Weight survey data accordingly.

source: Henrich, Heine, Norenzayan (2010) The weirdest people in the world?
finding: Behavioural science drew its samples mostly from WEIRD people, who are often outliers on perception, fairness, reasoning.
numbers: Background; not opened this session.
limits: From memory only.
agent_relevance: Origin of the critique that universals are assumed from WEIRD samples. Use as a caution flag.

source: Ji, Zhang, Nisbett (2004) Is it culture or is it language?
finding: Language of testing changed categorization in bilinguals, so culture and language effects can be confounded.
numbers: Seen only as a reference in Atari's list.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same confound appears in LLM work: prompt language is mixed with culture. Test both separately.

source: AlKhamissi et al. (2024) Investigating cultural alignment of LLMs
finding: Models align better with a culture when prompted in its dominant language and when pretrained on a mix with that language. Misalignment is worse for underrepresented personas and sensitive topics.
numbers: Replicates a survey in Egypt and the US with real respondent personas, Arabic and English prompts, models with different pretraining mixes.
limits: Two cultures only; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Real respondent personas are a stronger design than a country label.

source: Santurkar et al. (2023) Whose opinions do language models reflect?
finding: Model opinion distributions diverge from US groups; steering by demographic prompt gives only modest gains.
numbers: OpinionQA from Pew; representativeness metric defined over answer distributions.
limits: US only; numbers not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Even inside one country the default is not representative.

source: Synthesis across Durmus, Naous, Tao, Wang (this agent)
finding: Three controls recur: prompt language, explicit persona, in-context examples. Persona and examples beat language alone.
numbers: See c01 to c12.
limits: Synthesis by this agent, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: Where a scaffold needs culture-aware answers, use examples and persona, and check output with a rule.

source: Gap: no LLM test of Nisbett analytic vs holistic tasks found with numbers
finding: No primary LLM paper running the holistic/analytic tasks with numbers was found. arXiv, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar returned 429 and the shared web search budget ran out.
numbers: None.
limits: A gap, not evidence of absence.
agent_relevance: Needs follow-up; sibling subfield 01 may cover it.
